claim: Antagonistic receptive field surrounds are a near-universal property of early sensory processing.
source: Antagonistic receptive field surrounds are a near-universal property of early sensory processing.
evidence: This is a general statement about sensory processing that draws from established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: A key assumption in many models for retinal ganglion cell encoding is that receptive field surrounds are added only to the fully formed center signal.
source: A key assumption in many models for retinal ganglion cell encoding is that receptive field surrounds are added only to the fully formed center signal.
evidence: This claim is supported by references to existing modeling approaches in the field.

claim: Anatomical and functional observations indicate that surrounds are added before the summation of signals across receptive field subunits that creates the center.
source: But anatomical and functional observations indicate that surrounds are added before the summation of signals across receptive field subunits that creates the center.
evidence: This claim is based on prior anatomical and functional studies, as referenced throughout the manuscript.

claim: The surround can control sensitivity to fine spatial structure by changing the way the center integrates visual information over space.
source: Here, we show that this receptive field architecture has an important consequence for spatial contrast encoding in the macaque monkey retina: the surround can control sensitivity to fine spatial structure by changing the way the center integrates visual information over space.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The impact of the surround is particularly prominent when center and surround signals are correlated, as they are in natural stimuli.
source: The impact of the surround is particularly prominent when center and surround signals are correlated, as they are in natural stimuli.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing the effect of correlated center-surround signals.

claim: Natural scenes contain strong correlations across visual space.
source: Natural scenes contain strong correlations across visual space (Dong and Atick, 1995; Field, 1987; Simoncelli and Olshausen, 2001)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on natural scene statistics.

claim: The RF surround can decorrelate responses across a population of visual neurons.
source: and the RF surround can decorrelate responses across a population of visual neurons (Atick, 2011; Atick and Redlich, 1992; Dan et al., 1996)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior theoretical and experimental work.

claim: Mechanisms other than the surround can play a larger role in decorrelating population responses to natural images.
source: Recent findings have challenged this proposed function of the RF surround by showing that mechanisms other than the surround can play a larger role in decorrelating population responses to natural images. These include nonlinear processing in the retina (Pitkow and Meister, 2012) (see also [Franke et al., 2017; Maheswaranathan et al., 2017]) and fixational eye movements (Boi et al., 2017; Kuang et al., 2012; Rucci and Victor, 2015; Segal et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent studies that have challenged traditional views.

claim: Classical Difference-of-Gaussians and modern predictive RF models assume that the surround interacts only with the fully formed center signal.
source: Classical Difference-of-Gaussians (Enroth-Cugell and Lennie, 1975; Enroth-Cugell and Robson, 1966; Rodieck and Stone, 1965; Rodieck, 1965) and modern predictive RF models (Heitman et al., 2016; Pillow et al., 2008) assume that the surround interacts only with the fully formed center signal (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to classical and modern modeling approaches.

claim: Surrounds are generated by horizontal cells in the outer retina.
source: However, surrounds are generated by horizontal cells in the outer retina (Crook et al., 2011; Davenport et al., 2008; Mangel, 1991; McMahon et al., 2004; Verweij et al., 2003; Ströh et al., 2018; Drinnenberg et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior anatomical and functional studies.

claim: Surrounds are generated by amacrine cell feedback to bipolar cells in the inner retina.
source: and by amacrine cell feedback to bipolar cells in the inner retina (Cook and McReynolds, 1998; Farrow et al., 2013; Flores-Herr et al., 2001; Hoggarth et al., 2015; Taylor, 1999)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior anatomical and functional studies.

claim: At least a portion of the surround is present in the bipolar cells presynaptic to a RGC.
source: As a result, at least a portion of the surround is present in the bipolar cells presynaptic to a RGC (Figure 1C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1; [Dacey et al., 2000; Werblin and Dowling, 1969; Zhang et al., 2009; Borghuis et al., 2013; Franke et al., 2017; Buldyrev and Taylor, 2013])
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies and by reference to figures showing circuit organization.

claim: For many RGC types bipolar cells act as excitatory, nonlinear subunits within the RF center.
source: For many RGC types bipolar cells act as excitatory, nonlinear subunits within the RF center (Schwartz et al., 2012; Demb et al., 2001) (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies and by reference to a figure showing circuit organization.

claim: The degree of rectification at the bipolar cell to RGC synapse can control the spatial integration properties of the RF center.
source: The degree of rectification at the bipolar cell to RGC synapse can control the spatial integration properties of the RF center (Grimes et al., 2014; Turner and Rieke, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: A weakly rectified or linear synapse yields linear spatial integration due to cancellation of bright and dark regions of a scene.
source: In particular, a weakly rectified or linear synapse yields linear spatial integration due to cancellation of bright and dark regions of a scene
evidence: This claim is based on logical inference from the properties of linear systems and prior knowledge.

claim: A sharply rectified bipolar output synapse yields nonlinear spatial integration because light and dark regions fail to cancel.
source: whereas a sharply rectified bipolar output synapse yields nonlinear spatial integration because light and dark regions fail to cancel.
evidence: This claim is based on logical inference from the properties of nonlinear systems and prior knowledge.

claim: Nonlinear spatial integration causes RGCs to respond strongly to stimuli with fine spatial structure like gratings.
source: Nonlinear spatial integration causes RGCs to respond strongly to stimuli with fine spatial structure like gratings (Cafaro and Rieke, 2013; Crook et al., 2008; Enroth-Cugell and Robson, 1966; Hochstein and Shapley, 1976; Petrusca et al., 2007)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior experimental studies.

claim: Nonlinear spatial integration causes RGCs to respond strongly to natural images.
source: or natural images (Turner and Rieke, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: The nonlinear subunit structure of parasol RGCs has been well characterized.
source: The nonlinear subunit structure of these cells has been well characterized (Cafaro and Rieke, 2013; Crook et al., 2008; Petrusca et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The nonlinear structure of the RF center of Off-center parasol RGCs is important for encoding natural visual stimuli.
source: We focus on Off-center parasol RGCs in particular because the nonlinear structure of their RF center is important for encoding natural visual stimuli (Turner and Rieke, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: The linearity of spatial integration in the RF center depends on surround activation.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, we found that the linearity of spatial integration in the RF center depends on surround activation.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: Off parasol RGCs show stronger rectification of subunit output than On parasol cells.
source: We focused this test on Off parasol RGCs, because these cells show both stronger rectification of subunit output than On parasol cells (Chichilnisky and Kalmar, 2002)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: Off parasol RGCs show nonlinear spatial integration in the context of naturalistic visual stimuli.
source: and nonlinear spatial integration in the context of naturalistic visual stimuli (Turner and Rieke, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: Nonlinear spatial integration endows Off parasol RGCs with sensitivity to spatial contrast in natural images.
source: We previously found that nonlinear spatial integration endows Off parasol RGCs with sensitivity to spatial contrast in natural images (Turner and Rieke, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: Off parasol cells responded much more strongly to natural images than to linear equivalent stimuli, especially when the natural image contains high spatial contrast.
source: As shown previously, Off parasol cells responded much more strongly to natural images than to linear equivalent stimuli, especially when the natural image contains high spatial contrast (Figure 2A, left, Figure 2B; see also [Turner and Rieke, 2016]).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures and by citation to a prior study.

claim: When a bright surround was presented with the center stimulus, the natural image and its linear equivalent disc produced near-equal responses.
source: However, when a bright surround was presented with the center stimulus, the natural image and its linear equivalent disc produced near-equal responses (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Dark surrounds strongly suppressed both responses to natural images and linear equivalent discs.
source: Dark surrounds strongly suppressed both responses (Figure 2A, right).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in a figure.

claim: Spatial contrast sensitivity was maximal in response to stimuli for which center and surround intensities were similar.
source: Specifically, spatial contrast sensitivity was maximal in response to stimuli for which center and surround intensities were similar and dropped as intensity in these regions diverged.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Nonlinear spatial integration is maximized when center and surround experience similar mean luminance.
source: Hence, nonlinear spatial integration is maximized when center and surround experience similar mean luminance.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: When the surround strongly hyperpolarizes presynaptic bipolar cells, the response is diminished as a result of the surround shifting the synapse into a quiescent state.
source: When the surround strongly hyperpolarizes presynaptic bipolar cells (for Off cells, a dark surround), the response is diminished as a result of the surround shifting the synapse into a quiescent state.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data and knowledge of synaptic function.

claim: When the surround depolarizes presynaptic bipolar cells, the nonlinear sensitivity of the center is reduced.
source: When the surround depolarizes presynaptic bipolar cells (for Off cells, a bright surround), the nonlinear sensitivity of the center is reduced.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data and knowledge of synaptic function.

claim: The activity of the RF surround can control spatial integration by the center.
source: Hence, as in the hypothesis of Figure 1, these experiments indicate that the activity of the RF surround, rather than only interacting with the fully formed RF center signal, can control spatial integration by the center.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Off parasol RGCs respond strongly to split-field grating stimuli because of the nonlinear subunit structure of the RF center.
source: Because of the nonlinear subunit structure of the RF center, Off parasol cells respond strongly to such stimuli (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in a figure and by prior knowledge of RF structure.

claim: When paired with a bright surround, the grating stimulus did not activate the cell much beyond its response to the surround alone.
source: When paired with a bright surround, the grating stimulus did not activate the cell much beyond its response to the surround alone.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: A dark surround suppressed responses with and without the grating.
source: A dark surround suppressed responses with and without the grating, save for a small, brief response at the beginning of the presentation of the grating which is likely the result of the brief temporal delay of the surround relative to the center.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and inference about temporal dynamics.

claim: Nonlinear spatial integration is maximal when the center and surround experience the same mean luminance and decreases when the surround is brighter or dimmer than the center.
source: Thus, just as for natural image patches, nonlinear spatial integration is maximal when the center and surround experience the same mean luminance (in this case a mean of zero) and decreases when the surround is brighter or dimmer than the center.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Modulation of spatial integration by surround activity was similar in excitatory inputs and spike responses.
source: Modulation of spatial integration by surround activity was similar in excitatory inputs and spike responses (Figure 3E,F)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: The effect of the surround on spatial integration is already present in the bipolar synaptic output and is not substantially shaped by post-synaptic integration or spike generation mechanisms.
source: which indicates that it is already present in the bipolar synaptic output and is not substantially shaped by post-synaptic integration or spike generation mechanisms.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data comparing excitatory inputs and spike responses.

claim: A similar effect of the surround can be seen in the excitatory inputs to On parasol RGCs.
source: A similar effect can be seen in the excitatory inputs to On parasol RGCs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in a supplementary figure.

claim: The effect of the surround is not unique to the Off parasol excitatory pathway, but may be a more general feature of center-surround RF organization in the retina.
source: This shows that this effect of the surround is not unique to the Off parasol excitatory pathway, but may be a more general feature of center-surround RF organization in the retina.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing similar effects in On and Off parasol RGCs.

claim: On parasol RGCs are more easily shifted into a regime of linear spatial integration compared to Off parasol RGCs.
source: Compared to Off parasol RGCs, On parasol RGCs are more easily shifted into a regime of linear spatial integration, presumably because of the shallower rectification of nonlinear subunits in the receptive field of On parasol cells (Chichilnisky and Kalmar, 2002; Turner and Rieke, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citations to prior studies.

claim: Inputs to the RF surround can influence how the RF center integrates signals across space.
source: The experiments described in Figures 2 and 3 show that inputs to the RF surround can influence how the RF center integrates signals across space, consistent with the hypothesis outlined in Figure 1.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: For both the spike output and excitatory synaptic input to an Off parasol RGC, the peak spatial nonlinearity was observed when center and surround experienced similar mean luminance.
source: For both the spike output and excitatory synaptic input to an Off parasol RGC, the peak spatial nonlinearity was observed when center and surround experienced similar mean luminance (Figure 2C and Figure 3C,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: The shared model performed as well as the more complicated stacked model.
source: The shared model performed as well as the more complicated stacked model (Figure 4F), despite the latter having many more free parameters (10 free parameters) than the shared model (five free parameters).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of model performance on experimental data.

claim: The private nonlinearities fit in the stacked model tended to be quite shallow and much nearer to linear than the sharply rectified shared nonlinearity.
source: In addition, the private nonlinearities fit in the stacked model tended to be quite shallow and much nearer to linear than the sharply rectified shared nonlinearity (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of model parameters shown in a figure.

claim: The dominant nonlinear interaction between center and surround is characterized by a shared nonlinearity, and upstream of this nonlinearity center and surround interact approximately linearly.
source: The modeling result in Figure 4F supports the hypothesis that the dominant nonlinear interaction between center and surround is characterized by a shared nonlinearity, and that upstream of this nonlinearity center and surround interact approximately linearly.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results based on experimental data.

claim: The relationship between center activation and excitatory conductance depends on surround activation.
source: These joint response distributions show that the relationship between center activation and excitatory conductance depends on surround activation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: When the surround is only weakly activated, the nonlinear relationship between center activation and excitatory conductance is rectified.
source: When the surround is only weakly activated (near zero on 'surround' axis in Figure 5A), this nonlinear relationship is rectified (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Rectification persists when the surround hyperpolarizes presynaptic bipolar cells.
source: Rectification persists when the surround hyperpolarizes presynaptic bipolar cells (negative on 'surround' axis in Figure 5A, blue trace in Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: When the surround depolarizes bipolar cells, the relationship between center activation and excitatory conductance becomes more linear.
source: But when the surround depolarizes bipolar cells (positive on 'surround' axis in Figure 5A), the relationship between center activation and excitatory conductance becomes more linear (i.e. less rectified; Figure 5A,B, red trace).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: For both On and Off cells, rectification decreased as surround activation increased.
source: For both On and Off cells, rectification decreased as surround activation increased (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in a figure.

claim: Off cells were more rectified than On cells.
source: In agreement with previous observations (Chichilnisky and Kalmar, 2002; Turner and Rieke, 2016), Off cells were more rectified than On cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citations to prior studies.

claim: When center and surround nonlinearities are independent, the rectification of the center does not depend on the activity of the surround.
source: When center and surround nonlinearities are independent, the rectification of the center does not depend on the activity of the surround because the surround enters only after the center is fully formed (horizontal gray line in inset).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the properties of the independent nonlinearity model.

claim: The shared nonlinearity model predicts a decrease in rectification as the surround becomes more depolarizing, in agreement with the behavior of parasol RGCs.
source: The shared nonlinearity model, on the other hand, predicts a decrease in rectification as the surround becomes more depolarizing, in agreement with the behavior of parasol RGCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of model predictions with experimental data.

claim: For both spike and excitatory current responses, the measured center-surround response was smaller than the linear sum of the two responses measured independently.
source: For both spike and excitatory current responses, the measured center-surround response was smaller than the linear sum of the two responses measured independently.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: RF center and surround interact nonlinearly.
source: Thus, RF center and surround interact nonlinearly.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing sublinear summation.

claim: The nonlinear interaction between center and surround is present in the excitatory synaptic input, and hence reflects properties of bipolar synaptic output rather than nonlinearities in synaptic integration or spike generation in the ganglion cell.
source: This interaction, like that in Figure 4 and 5, is present in the excitatory synaptic input, and hence reflects properties of bipolar synaptic output rather than nonlinearities in synaptic integration or spike generation in the ganglion cell.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data comparing excitatory inputs and spike responses.

claim: Sublinear interactions between center and surround held across cells and fixations for both spike output and excitatory synaptic input.
source: Sublinear interactions between center and surround inputs held across cells and fixations for both spike output (Figure 6E) and excitatory synaptic input (Figure 6F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: For each cell, the difference between the linear sum of responses to center and surround inputs and the measured simultaneous response for spike outputs was correlated with the same difference for excitatory inputs.
source: For each cell, the difference between the linear sum of responses to center and surround inputs and the measured simultaneous response for spike outputs was correlated with the same difference for excitatory inputs (Figure 6G,H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: The nonlinear interaction seen at the level of spike output is largely inherited from the excitatory synaptic inputs.
source: This is consistent with the interpretation that the nonlinear interaction seen at the level of spike output is largely inherited from the excitatory synaptic inputs.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the correlation between spike and excitatory input nonlinearities.

claim: Sublinear interactions in spike output and excitatory synaptic input were more strongly correlated for Off than On parasol RGCs.
source: Sublinear interactions in spike output and excitatory synaptic input were more strongly correlated for Off than On parasol RGCs (Figure 6H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in a figure.

claim: Inhibitory input impacts On parasol responses to natural stimuli more than Off parasol responses.
source: This may be because inhibitory input impacts On parasol responses to natural stimuli more than Off parasol responses (Turner and Rieke, 2016).
evidence: This claim is based on inference and citation to a prior study.

claim: The nonlinear center-surround interactions characterized in Figures 2–5 are prominent for naturalistic visual inputs.
source: Taken together, these observations demonstrate that the nonlinear center-surround interactions characterized in Figures 2–5 are prominent for naturalistic visual inputs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Naturalistic center and surround stimuli tended to elicit responses at different times.
source: Naturalistic center and surround stimuli tended to elicit responses at different times (Figure 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in a figure.

claim: The spatial correlations in intensity that characterize natural images are consistent with the antagonistic nature of the surround.
source: This is consistent with the spatial correlations in intensity that characterize natural images (Simoncelli and Olshausen, 2001) and the antagonistic nature of the surround
evidence: This claim is based on inference from natural image statistics and knowledge of surround properties.

claim: When spatial correlations were intact, inputs to the center and surround combined sub-linearly in the excitatory synaptic input to the cell.
source: When spatial correlations were intact, inputs to the center and surround combined sub-linearly in the excitatory synaptic input to the cell (Figure 7D)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in a figure.

claim: When surround intensities were shuffled relative to the center, nonlinear center-surround interactions were much weaker.
source: When we shuffled the surround intensities relative to the center, nonlinear center-surround interactions were much weaker (Figure 7E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Nonlinear center-surround interactions depend on the correlation between center and surround inputs.
source: These results indicate that nonlinear center-surround interactions depend strongly on center-surround intensity correlations, and hence that the importance of these interactions could be underestimated from stimuli such as spatial noise that lack intensity correlations.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: When noise stimuli in the center and surround were negatively correlated, inputs to the center and surround summed linearly or very nearly so.
source: When noise stimuli in the center and surround were negatively correlated, inputs to the center and surround summed linearly or very nearly so (Figure 7H, left).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in a figure.

claim: As the center-surround intensity correlations increased, sublinear interactions became more obvious.
source: As the center-surround intensity correlations increased, sublinear interactions became more obvious (Figure 7H, middle and right).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in a figure.

claim: Strongly positively correlated noise stimuli induced center-surround interactions that resembled those seen using naturally correlated luminance stimuli.
source: Strongly positively correlated noise stimuli induced center-surround interactions that resembled those seen using naturally correlated luminance stimuli (Figure 7H, right).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in a figure.

claim: Surround signals can alter how the center integrates over space rather than only interacting with the fully formed center signal.
source: The experiments described above show that surround signals, rather than only interacting with the fully formed center signal, can alter how the center integrates over space.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Natural stimuli elicit strong nonlinear center-surround interactions due to positive correlations between center and surround intensities.
source: natural stimuli elicit strong nonlinear center-surround interactions due to positive correlations between center and surround intensities (Figures 6 and 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Surround activation can make spatial integration in the RF center relatively insensitive to changes in mean luminance.
source: These observations lead to the hypothesis, tested below, that surround activation can make spatial integration in the RF center relatively insensitive to changes in mean luminance.
evidence: This is a hypothesis that is tested with experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: A decrease in mean luminance over the RF center will depolarize the synapse associated with each RF subunit, shifting each into a locally linear state, and decreasing spatial contrast sensitivity.
source: A decrease in mean luminance over the RF center will depolarize the synapse associated with each RF subunit, shifting each into a locally linear state (Figure 8A, top), and decreasing spatial contrast sensitivity.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from knowledge of synaptic function and is illustrated in a figure.

claim: When a center stimulus is paired with a luminance-matched surround stimulus, the antagonistic surround may at least partially cancel depolarization and preserve spatial contrast sensitivity.
source: When such a stimulus is paired with a luminance-matched surround stimulus, the antagonistic surround may at least partially cancel this depolarization; this could keep each subunit in a locally rectified state (Figure 8A, bottom, blue arrow) and preserve spatial contrast sensitivity.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from knowledge of surround function and is illustrated in a figure.

claim: A grating with a dark mean luminance signal produced a similar response as a linear equivalent stimulus, indicating that the cell is insensitive to the spatial contrast present in the grating.
source: A grating with a dark mean luminance signal produced a similar response as a linear equivalent stimulus (Figure 8B, left), indicating that the cell is insensitive to the spatial contrast present in the grating.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in a figure.

claim: When a dark mean grating is paired with a luminance-matched surround, the grating again produces a much stronger response than its linear equivalent stimulus, consistent with the restoration of spatial contrast sensitivity.
source: When a dark mean grating is paired with a luminance-matched surround, however, the grating again produces a much stronger response than its linear equivalent stimulus (Figure 8B, middle), which is consistent with the restoration of spatial contrast sensitivity via the mechanism in Figure 8A.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in a figure.

claim: Pairing the grating stimulus with poorly matched surrounds does not restore spatial contrast sensitivity.
source: Pairing the grating stimulus with poorly matched surrounds does not restore spatial contrast sensitivity (Figure 8B, right), indicating that this is not a general consequence of surround activation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in a figure.

claim: The NLI was maximal for all surround conditions for zero-mean gratings.
source: The NLI was maximal for all surround conditions for zero-mean gratings.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: As the center intensity decreased, the NLI decreased along with it, but this drop was less pronounced under the matched surround condition.
source: As the center intensity decreased (moving towards the left in Figure 8C), the NLI decreased along with it, but this drop was less pronounced under the matched surround condition.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in a figure.

claim: Matched surround activation decreased the sensitivity of nonlinear spatial integration to changes in mean luminance.
source: Hence matched surround activation decreased the sensitivity of nonlinear spatial integration to changes in mean luminance.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The intensity correlations present in natural images should ensure that the mean intensity difference between the RF center and surround is often near zero.
source: The intensity correlations present in natural images (e.g. Figure 7C) should ensure that the mean intensity difference between the RF center and surround is often near zero.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from natural image statistics.

claim: Full natural image stimulation of the RF surround would increase spatial contrast sensitivity in the RF center compared to stimulation of the RF center alone.
source: Because spatial contrast sensitivity was maximized by small differences between mean center and surround intensity (Figure 2), we hypothesized that full natural image stimulation of the RF surround would increase spatial contrast sensitivity in the RF center compared to stimulation of the RF center alone.
evidence: This is a hypothesis that is tested with experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: A darker mean luminance signal was associated with a decrease in spatial contrast sensitivity.
source: As in the modified gratings experiments (Figure 8C), a darker mean luminance signal was associated with a decrease in spatial contrast sensitivity (Figure 8F, black curve).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in a figure.

claim: The drop-off in spatial contrast sensitivity was less pronounced with the naturally occurring surround.
source: This drop-off in spatial contrast sensitivity was less pronounced with the naturally occurring surround, (Figure 8F, blue curve).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in a figure.

claim: Sensitivity to fine spatial structure was two to three times greater in the presence of a matched surround than without a surround.
source: Specifically, sensitivity to fine spatial structure was two to three times greater in the presence of a matched surround than without a surround.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Randomly selected surrounds did not enhance spatial contrast sensitivity but instead altered the NLI in a manner predicted by the experiments in Figure 2.
source: Randomly selected surrounds did not enhance spatial contrast sensitivity in this way but instead altered the NLI in a manner predicted by the experiments in Figure 2 (see Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in a supplementary figure.

claim: Natural images provide inputs to the surround that can preserve the spatial contrast sensitivity of the RF center compared to center inputs alone.
source: These observations are consistent with the idea that natural images provide inputs to the surround that can preserve the spatial contrast sensitivity of the RF center compared to center inputs alone.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: Key to the relative invariance of contrast sensitivity is the ability of the surround to control the degree of rectification of the bipolar subunits that comprise the RF center and the strong positive correlations between center and surround inputs created by natural images.
source: Key to this relative invariance of contrast sensitivity is the ability of the surround to control the degree of rectification of the bipolar subunits that comprise the RF center and the strong positive correlations between center and surround inputs created by natural images.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data and modeling results.

claim: The NLI is, on average, lower for randomly selected images than for grating stimuli.
source: Note, however, that the NLI is, on average, lower for randomly selected images than for grating stimuli (compare Figure 8F and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of experimental data shown in figures.

claim: The spatial structure of grating stimuli is designed to highlight nonlinear spatial integration by differentially activating subunits in the RF center.
source: This is expected because the spatial structure of grating stimuli is designed to highlight nonlinear spatial integration by differentially activating subunits in the RF center (i.e. depolarizing some while hyperpolarizing others).
evidence: This claim is based on knowledge of how grating stimuli interact with RF structure.

claim: Randomly-selected image patches often do not contain much spatial structure that will differentially activate subunits in the RF center.
source: Randomly-selected image patches, however, often do not contain much spatial structure that will differentially activate subunits in the RF center.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the properties of natural images.

claim: The inclusion of the naturally occurring surround extended spatial contrast sensitivity in the face of stronger local luminance signals in the RF model.
source: As in the Off parasol spike data, the inclusion of the naturally occurring surround extended spatial contrast sensitivity in the face of stronger local luminance signals.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results.

claim: A stronger RF surround is associated with greater spatial contrast sensitivity, especially for images that contain a strong local luminance signal.
source: A stronger RF surround is associated with greater spatial contrast sensitivity, especially for images that contain a strong local luminance signal.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results.

claim: Visual inputs to the RF surround can change how the RF center integrates inputs across space, including in natural scenes.
source: Here, we have shown that visual inputs to the RF surround can change how the RF center integrates inputs across space, including in natural scenes.
evidence: This is a summary of the primary findings of the study.

claim: During natural vision, the local luminance experienced by a RGC can vary dramatically from fixation to fixation.
source: During natural vision, the local luminance experienced by a RGC can vary dramatically from fixation to fixation (van Hateren et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: Sensitivity to small scale spatial contrast relies critically on the rectification of bipolar subunit outputs.
source: Because sensitivity to small scale (sub-RF center) spatial contrast relies critically on the rectification of bipolar subunit outputs
evidence: This claim is based on knowledge from prior studies.

claim: Changes in luminance and corresponding changes in bipolar voltage could prevent a RGC that responds nonlinearly to grating stimuli from detecting spatial contrast present in natural images.
source: these changes in luminance and corresponding changes in bipolar voltage could prevent a RGC that responds nonlinearly to grating stimuli from detecting spatial contrast present in natural images.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from knowledge of RF function.

claim: The incorporation of an antagonistic surround before formation of the nonlinear center ensures that the effect of the mean intensity signal is partially mitigated for natural scenes and other stimuli with strong spatial correlations in intensity.

source: This mechanism is in line with the surround's classical role in reducing sensitivity to changes in mean luminance via subtraction

claim: The mechanism has the additional consequence of reducing the dependence of spatial contrast sensitivity on mean luminance by controlling the set point of the bipolar cell nonlinearity.

claim: The extent to which spatial contrast sensitivity is preserved will depend on the strength of the surround.

evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data and modeling results, and is supported by a citation.

claim: For regions of an image where the center and surround luminance signals are very different, a nonlinear RGC will lose much of its small-scale spatial contrast sensitivity and instead encode input with a spatial scale dictated by the classical center-surround RF.
source: For those (relatively rare) regions of an image where the center and surround luminance signals are very different, a nonlinear RGC will lose much of its small-scale spatial contrast sensitivity and instead encode input with a spatial scale dictated by the classical center-surround RF.

claim: The inclusion of nonlinear subunits in the RF center is important to capture responses to spatially structured stimuli.
source: Past work in parasol RGCs as well as other RGC types has shown that the inclusion of nonlinear subunits in the RF center is important to capture responses to spatially structured stimuli (Bölinger and Gollisch, 2012; Crook et al., 2008; Demb et al., 1999; Freeman et al., 2015; Schwartz et al., 2012), including natural scenes (Turner and Rieke, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The results rely on nonlinear subunits in the RF center having a center-surround RF organization.
source: The results shown here rely on nonlinear subunits in the RF center having a center-surround RF organization.

claim: The surround is present in diffuse bipolar cells in primate retina.

claim: Capturing RGC center-surround interactions and spatial contrast sensitivity will require incorporating the impact of the surround on subunits within the receptive field center.
source: The work presented here indicates that capturing RGC center-surround interactions and spatial contrast sensitivity will require incorporating the impact of the surround on subunits within the receptive field center.

source: If nonlinear spatial integration substantially shapes surround suppression, then the spatial structure of the surround should contribute to center-surround interactions.
